summary:
Burdur Province sits under Türkiye's national legal and policing framework, which provides no scope for a separate provincial regime. The Turkish Criminal Code applies as written. Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with penalties of up to three years in prison, and to criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care, including surgery, from 18 to 25 and require permanent infertility as a condition, and would punish health professionals who provide such care. The package had not been adopted when reported. Its pending status has not prevented authorities from acting as though the prohibitions already operate.

Human Rights Watch describes the draft as one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades. Fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose it, which indicates organised domestic resistance but no current legal shield for a visitor.

Kaos GL's 2025 report, launched under the title 'A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy', records 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, alongside 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. The report finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people has been institutionalised as explicit state policy: senior officials' hate speech, instructions issued to public institutions under a 'Year of the Family' banner, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom. Findings were presented at the launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen.

Street-level enforcement illustrates the gap between draft text and practice. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly twenty trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that police took no fines but documented them anyway, and that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

The document-carrying rule compounds that exposure. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events remain flashpoints. Monitoring by the Truth Justice Memory Center of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated demands for an independent investigation came from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın. Accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that Türkiye places trans prisoners by registered sex — a trans man had been held in a women's prison — and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. No policy or staff training exists to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

The pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
tangentialFactors:
The draft package is contested inside Türkiye as well as abroad. Fifteen Turkish LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the 11th Judicial Package, and opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised a trans prisoner's death in parliament on 12 December 2025. Contestation has not produced a suspension of enforcement practice.

Legal argument against the checkpoint regime runs through the European Convention on Human Rights. Experts cited in the reporting on the Beyoğlu GBT stops hold that the checks breach Article 5, which protects against arbitrary deprivation of liberty. Türkiye is a party to that convention, so the argument is available to a detained visitor, though the reporting gives no instance of it succeeding at the point of stop.

Monitoring infrastructure exists and is active: Kaos GL counts violations annually, the Truth Justice Memory Center observes Pride weeks, the Human Rights Association coordinates across six cities, and Prison Insider profiles detention conditions with ILGA World data. These bodies document rather than prevent, and their coverage is concentrated in large cities rather than in provinces such as Burdur.

Historical depth matters for expectation-setting. Human Rights Watch's 2008 findings on beatings, robberies and abuse predate the post-2018 legal changes and should be read as evidence of how long the hostility has persisted, not as a statement of the law now in force.
localsOnly:
Kaos GL's 2025 report was presented at a public launch by lawyer Kerem Dikmen, and its framing — hostility turned into state policy — reflects findings that Turkish civil society has been able to publish and circulate domestically despite the restrictive climate.

Instructions issued to public institutions under the 'Year of the Family' banner affect residents directly, shaping how state employees, schools and public bodies treat LGBT people. Regulatory and supervisory bodies restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom bear on residents' work, publishing and performance.

Residents hold a national identity card rather than a passport for domestic checkpoints, so the original-photo-ID rule and its 3,000 lira fine apply to foreign nationals. The practical document exposure at a Burdur checkpoint is therefore different for a Turkish citizen than for a visitor.

Access to transition-related care runs through medical boards. The Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular adding 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for board reports, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation requiring e-reports and barring the 'other' option, govern the records Turkish patients generate when seeking care.

Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın coordinate on prison deaths, and lawyers and visiting prisoners can give accounts of custody conditions. Complaint mechanisms inside prisons are described as ineffective and capable of provoking further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a trans-specific incident, police stop, detention or prosecution in Burdur Province itself. The province-level picture is inferred from national law and national enforcement reporting, and Burdur-specific practice is unresolved.

The adoption status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved. Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and it had not been passed at that point; no later source in the inventory confirms whether it has since been enacted, amended or withdrawn.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri circular apply to health facilities in Burdur is not sourced here. The Kayseri circular is a provincial instrument from another province, and no Burdur Provincial Health Directorate documentation is available in this inventory.

The inventory contains no data on detention facilities in Burdur Province, no record of how trans detainees would be classified there, and no Burdur-specific reporting on Pride or assembly restrictions. The prison findings derive from a national profile and from the Sincan case near Ankara.

Whether the fines and detention warnings attached to the photo-ID rule have been applied to foreign visitors in Burdur is not sourced. The 3,000 lira figure and the checkpoint practice are reported nationally, without provincial breakdown.
